newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan hog crisis seen benefiting US, Canada.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan hog crisis seen benefiting US, Canada.

text.p: Taiwan's ban on pork exports has sent the domestic industry into crisis and U.S. and Canadian breeders are most likely to benefit, experts said on Friday.
"Taiwan's pork export market will be replaced by other competitors," said Jack Lee at Taiwan's Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Corp, a livestock and feed company.
"U.S. and Canadian breeders should be happy now."
Japan, Taiwan's largest pork export market, on Friday imposed an indefinite ban on pork shipments from Taiwan after an outbreak of foot and mouth disease.
South Korea, which imported 1,497 tonnes of pork from Taiwan in 1996, also announced a ban on cloven-hoofed animals and products imported from Taiwan.
Tokyo traders said alternative pork suppliers were the United States, Canada and Europe.

"Canada's pork export capacity is limited, and European pork takes a longer shipment period. So the U.S. will be the most likely source to fulfill Taiwan's losses," a pork trader at Japan's major trading house said.

Japan had been importing some 16,000 tonnes of fresh and frozen pork from Taiwan a month despite Tokyo's imposition of a special "emergency" import tariff to limit imports and protect local breeders, Taiwan traders said.
Japan imported about 183,494 tonnes of pork from Taiwan in 1995, ranking Taiwan as its largest supplier, they said.
Taiwan Sugar, one of the island's major hog breeders, said exports could be halted for years.
"We can only hope that Taiwan can resume exports within three years," Taiwan Sugar director Stella Yuan said by telephone.
Yuan said the crisis would force many smaller hog breeders out of businesses.
"Smaller breeding farms will certainly try other agricultural products or go bankrupt," Yuan said.
Taiwan's wholesale pork prices plummeted by as much as 61 percent in Thursday night trading after the government announced the export ban.
The average wholesale pork price in southern Taiwan was quoted at T$18 (65.4 U.S. cents) on Thursday, down from T$46 (US$1.67) on Wednesday.
Taiwan's upset breeders said the ban had sent the industry into chaos without any warning.
"The government should inform breeders before announcing a ban," a breeder said. "The falling pork prices will kill us."
Local media reported on Friday nine small breeding farms had already said they were going out of business and considering other agricultural products.
Taiwan's Council of Agriculture banned all pork exports on Thursday following the outbreak of the deadly contagious foot and mouth disease in the island's large hog population.
The council estimated that Taiwan exported six million out of the 14 million hogs it bred per year.

According to a council survey in 1994, the hog industry's net value stood at T$89 billion (US$3.24 billion), comprising 20 percent of Taiwan's farm production value and 60 percent of the livestock sector.
The island faced a daunting task in trying to eliminate the disease and would import two million doses of vaccine to combat the outbreak, the council said.
The export ban would also hurt many of Taiwan's pork-related downstream businesses, particularly the feed industry.

A survey of five major Taiwan grain importers found that all expected significant reductions in corn imports, with most estimating the downturn at about 1.2 million tonnes or 19 percent of the island's annual imports of 6.5 million tonnes.
